lessons.title: Cell Structure and Microscopy
lessons.content: Eukaryotic and Prokaryotic Cells All living things are made of cells. Cells are divided into two fundamental types: eukaryotic cells and prokaryotic cells. Understanding the differences between these two types is a key part of AQA and regularly tested in exams. Eukaryotic cells include both animal and plant cells. They have a nucleus that encloses their genetic material, along with other membrane-bound organelle s such as mitochondria and ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells — bacteria — are much smaller and simpler. They lack a true nucleus: instead, their genetic material is a single loop of DNA that floats freely in the cytoplasm. Prokaryotes may also contain small rings of extra DNA called plasmid s. Key Fact Eukaryotic cells (animal and plant) have a nucleus that encloses their DNA. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no true nucleus — their DNA is a single loop in the cytoplasm, and they may also contain plasmids. A typical animal cell is around 10–30 µm (micrometres) in diameter. A prokaryotic bacterial cell is much smaller, typically 1–5 µm. You need to be comfortable with order of magnitude calculations using standard form, and the prefixes centi (10 −2 ), milli (10 −3 ), micro (10 −6 ) and nano (10 −9 ). Animal and Plant Cells Both animal and plant cells are eukaryotic, but they contain different organelles. You must be able to name each organelle and explain how its structure relates to its function. Animal Cell Organelles and Their Functions Nucleus — contains the cell’s genetic material (DNA) and controls the cell’s activities. The DNA carries the instructions for making proteins. Cytoplasm — a jelly-like substance where most chemical reactions take place. Enzymes in the cytoplasm control these metabolic reactions. Cell membrane — a thin layer that surrounds the cell and controls which substances enter and leave. It is selectively permeable. Mitochondria — the site of aerobic respiration, where energy is transferred from glucose. Cells that need lots of energy (such as muscle cells) contain more mitochondria. Ribosomes — tiny structures in the cytoplasm where protein synthesis occurs. They are found in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells. Plant cells have all of the organelles listed above, plus three additional structures: Chloroplasts — contain the green pigment chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis . They absorb light energy to make glucose. Permanent vacuole — a large, fluid-filled space containing cell sap (a weak solution of sugars and salts). It helps keep the cell rigid and supports the plant. Cell wall — made of cellulose and surrounds the cell membrane. It strengthens and supports the cell, preventing it from bursting when water enters by osmosis. Key Fact Plant cells have a cell wall (cellulose), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a permanent vacuole (cell sap) in addition to the organelles found in animal cells. Bacterial cells have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, no true nucleus and no mitochondria. Cell Specialisation Not every cell in an organism looks the same. Cells become specialised — they develop particular structures that allow them to perform a specific function. The exam regularly asks you to explain how a cell’s structure relates to its function. Examples of Specialised Cells Sperm cell — has a streamlined head, a long tail (flagellum) for swimming, and many mitochondria to provide energy for movement. It carries the male DNA to the egg. Nerve cell — has a long axon to carry electrical impulses over long distances, branched endings (dendrites) to connect with other nerve cells, and a myelin sheath to insulate the signal and speed up transmission. Muscle cell — contains many mitochondria to supply energy for contraction. Muscle cells are elongated so they can contract and relax to produce movement. Root hair cell — has a long, thin extension (the root hair) that increases the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil. Xylem cell — a hollow, dead tube reinforced with lignin that transports water and mineral ions from roots to leaves in a continuous column. Phloem cell — has sieve plates with pores that allow dissolved sugars to flow through the plant from leaves to other parts (translocation). Cell Differentiation The process by which a cell becomes specialised is called differentiation . As a cell differentiates, it acquires the sub-cellular structures it needs for its function. Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage of development. Once they have specialised, they generally cannot change into a different cell type, and cell division in mature animals is mainly for repair and replacement. Plant cells, however, retain the ability to differentiate throughout their lives . This is why you can take a cutting from a plant and it will grow into a new individual. Key Fact Animal cells differentiate early and are then permanently specialised. Plant cells can differentiate throughout life — this is why cuttings can grow into new plants. Microscopy Microscopes allow us to see cells and sub-cellular structures that are invisible to the naked eye. There are two main types you need to know about: light microscopes and electron microscopes . Light microscopes use glass lenses and visible light to produce a magnified image. They have a maximum useful magnification of about ×1,500 and a resolution (the ability to distinguish two close points as separate) of around 200 nm. Light microscopes were first developed in the 1590s and allowed scientists to discover cells for the first time. Electron microscopes fire a beam of electrons at the specimen rather than using light. They have a much higher resolution (down to about 0.2 nm) and a useful magnification of up to ×2,000,000. This allows biologists to see sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and the internal structure of mitochondria in much finer detail. The Magnification Formula You must be able to use the magnification formula: \(magnification = \text{size of image} \div \text{size of real object}\) This can be rearranged using a formula triangle. If the image of a cell is 30 mm across and the real cell is 0.03 mm (30 µm), then: magnification = 30 ÷ 0.03 = ×1,000. Always check both measurements are in the same units before dividing. Express very large or very small answers in standard form where appropriate. lessons.title: Cell Division and Transport
lessons.content: Chromosomes and the Genetic Material The nucleus of every cell contains thread-like structures called chromosomes . Each chromosome is a long molecule of DNA, and each chromosome carries a large number of genes. In body cells, chromosomes are found in pairs — human body cells contain 23 pairs, giving 46 chromosomes in total. Key Fact Human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in total). Each chromosome is made of DNA and carries many genes . The Cell Cycle and Mitosis Cells divide in a series of stages called the cell cycle . The cell cycle allows organisms to grow, repair damaged tissue, and replace worn-out cells. Before a cell divides, it must prepare by growing larger and increasing the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria. The DNA then replicates so that each chromosome is copied, producing two identical copies. The stage of the cell cycle where the cell actually divides its nucleus is called mitosis . During mitosis, one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides. Finally, the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to form two identical daughter cells. Each new cell has exactly the same number of chromosomes — and exactly the same genetic information — as the original parent cell. The Three Stages of the Cell Cycle Stage 1 — Growth and DNA replication: The cell grows, increases the number of sub-cellular structures (e.g. mitochondria, ribosomes), and the DNA replicates to form two copies of each chromosome. Stage 2 — Mitosis: One set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides into two. Stage 3 — Division: The cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to produce two identical daughter cells. In plant cells, a new cell wall also forms. Key Fact You need to know the three overall stages of the cell cycle, but you do not need to name the individual phases of mitosis (prophase, metaphase, etc.). Stem Cells A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce many more cells of the same type. Certain stem cells can also differentiate into specialised cell types. There are three main sources of stem cells that The specification requires you to know. Embryonic stem cells are found in early human embryos. They can differentiate into almost any type of human cell, making them extremely useful for medical research. Adult stem cells are found in bone marrow and can form many types of cells, including blood cells, but they are more limited than embryonic stem cells. Meristem tissue in plants contains stem cells that can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the plant’s life. Uses, Risks, and Ethical Issues of Stem Cells Medical uses: Stem cell treatments may help conditions such as diabetes and paralysis. In therapeutic cloning, an embryo is produced with the same genes as the patient, so stem cells from it are not rejected by the patient’s immune system. Risks: There is a potential risk of transferring viral infections through stem cell treatments. Ethical objections: Some people object to embryonic stem cell research because it involves the destruction of a human embryo, which they consider to be a potential human life. Others argue the potential to save lives justifies the research. Plant stem cells: Meristem cells can be used to produce clones of plants quickly and economically. This is used to clone rare species to protect them from extinction and to produce large numbers of crop plants with desirable features such as disease resistance. Diffusion Diffusion is the spreading out of particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. It is a passive process — it does not require energy from the cell. Important examples of diffusion in biology include oxygen and carbon dioxide moving in and out of cells during gas exchange, and the waste product urea moving from cells into the blood plasma for excretion by the kidneys. Key Fact Three factors affect the rate of diffusion: the concentration gradient (difference in concentration), the temperature , and the surface area of the membrane. A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio , allowing sufficient transport of molecules by diffusion alone. Multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces (such as the lungs, small intestine, gills, roots, and leaves) because their surface area to volume ratio is much smaller relative to their needs. These exchange surfaces are adapted by having a large surface area, thin membranes for a short diffusion path, a rich blood supply, and ventilation. Osmosis Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution (where water molecules are in higher concentration) to a concentrated solution (where water molecules are in lower concentration) through a partially permeable membrane . Like diffusion, osmosis is a passive process and does not require energy from respiration. Required Practical: Investigating Osmosis AQA Required Practical 3 involves investigating the effect of a range of concentrations of salt or sugar solutions on the mass of plant tissue (usually potato cylinders). You measure the mass before and after placing the tissue in each solution, then calculate percentage change in mass. In dilute solutions, the tissue gains mass by osmosis (water enters the cells). In concentrated solutions, it loses mass (water leaves the cells). You should be able to plot and interpret graphs of percentage mass change against solution concentration. Active Transport Active transport moves substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution — this means it works against the concentration gradient. Unlike diffusion and osmosis, active transport requires energy from respiration . There are two key examples the specification requires. First, active transport allows mineral ions to be absorbed into plant root hair cells from very dilute solutions in the soil — plants need these minerals for healthy growth. Second, it allows sugar molecules to be absorbed from the gut into the blood, even though the blood already has a higher sugar concentration than the gut contents. The sugar is then used for cell respiration. Key Fact The three transport processes compared: Diffusion — high to low concentration, passive (no energy). Osmosis — water only, dilute to concentrated through a partially permeable membrane, passive. Active transport —

lessons.title: Organisation and the Digestive System
lessons.content: Principles of Organisation The human body is organised into a hierarchy of structures, each more complex than the last. Cells are the basic building blocks of all living organisms. A group of cells with a similar structure and function is called a tissue . Tissues are grouped together to form organs , and organs are organised into organ systems . The digestive system is a perfect example of an organ system — several different organs work together to digest food and absorb the nutrients the body needs. Understanding this hierarchy (cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism) is essential for AQA Biology, as it shows how the body is organised to carry out complex functions efficiently. Key Fact The hierarchy of organisation in the body is: \(cells \rightarrow tissues \rightarrow organs \rightarrow \text{organ systems} \rightarrow organism\) . The digestive system is an organ system in which the stomach, small intestine, pancreas, liver, and other organs work together to break down and absorb food. The Human Digestive System The role of the digestive system is to break down large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream and transported to cells. This process involves both mechanical digestion (physical breakdown by chewing and churning) and chemical digestion (breakdown by enzymes ). Key Organs of the Digestive System The digestive system includes the following organs, each with a specific role: Mouth: Food is chewed into smaller pieces (mechanical digestion) and mixed with saliva , which contains the enzyme amylase. This begins the chemical digestion of starch into sugars. Oesophagus: A muscular tube that pushes food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis (waves of muscle contraction). Stomach: A muscular organ that churns food and mixes it with hydrochloric acid and protease enzymes . The acid kills bacteria and provides the acidic pH (around pH 2) that stomach proteases need to work. Small intestine: Where the final stages of chemical digestion occur and where the products of digestion are absorbed into the bloodstream. The inner wall is covered in tiny finger-like projections called villi , which increase the surface area for absorption. Large intestine: Absorbs water from undigested food, forming solid faeces. Pancreas: A gland that produces protease, lipase, and amylase enzymes, which are released into the small intestine. Liver: Produces bile , which is stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine. Enzymes and Digestion Digestive enzymes are biological catalysts — they speed up the breakdown of large food molecules without being used up themselves. Each enzyme has a specifically shaped active site that fits only one type of substrate, like a lock and key. This is called the lock and key theory . There are three main groups of digestive enzymes, and you must know what each one does, where it is produced, and what it breaks food down into: Key Fact Amylase (a carbohydrase) breaks down starch into simple sugars (maltose/glucose). It is produced in the salivary glands , the pancreas , and the small intestine . Key Fact Proteases break down proteins into amino acids. They are produced in the stomach (pepsin, which works best in acidic conditions), the pancreas , and the small intestine . Key Fact Lipases break down lipids (fats and oils) into glycerol and fatty acids. They are produced in the pancreas and the small intestine . The Role of Bile Bile plays a crucial role in digestion, even though it is not an enzyme. It is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder . When food enters the small intestine, bile is released and has two important functions: 1. Neutralisation: Bile is alkaline , so it neutralises the hydrochloric acid that comes from the stomach. This is important because enzymes in the small intestine work best in slightly alkaline conditions (around pH 7–8). Without bile, the acid from the stomach would make the pH too low for these enzymes to function. 2. Emulsification of fats: Bile emulsifies fats — it breaks large fat globules into much smaller droplets. This massively increases the surface area of the fat, giving lipase enzymes a much larger area to work on. This speeds up the rate of fat digestion. Why Surface Area Matters for Digestion Enzymes can only work on the surface of food molecules. When bile breaks large fat globules into tiny droplets, the total surface area exposed to lipase increases dramatically. Think of it like this: a whole block of butter has a small surface area, but if you broke it into thousands of tiny pieces, the combined surface area would be far greater. More surface area means more lipase molecules can bind to fat at the same time, so digestion happens much faster. Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity Enzymes are proteins, and their activity is affected by temperature and pH . Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH at which it works fastest. If the temperature is too low , molecules move slowly and collide with the active site less frequently, so the reaction rate is low. As temperature increases, molecules move faster and collide more often, increasing the rate. At the optimum temperature (around 37°C for most human enzymes), the rate is at its maximum. If the temperature rises above the optimum , the enzyme’s active site changes shape — the enzyme is denatured . The substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme can no longer catalyse the reaction. Denaturation is permanent. Similarly, extreme changes in pH can denature enzymes. Stomach protease (pepsin) works best at pH 2 (very acidic), while enzymes in the small intestine work best at around pH 7–8 (slightly alkaline). This is why bile’s role in neutralising stomach acid is so important. Required Practical: Investigating pH and Amylase AQA Required Practical 5 asks you to investigate how pH affects the rate of amylase activity. You add amylase to a starch solution at different pH values (using buffer solutions) and sample the mixture every 30 seconds using iodine reagent . Iodine turns blue-black in the presence of starch. When the iodine no longer changes colour, all the starch has been digested. You record the time taken at each pH and use it to calculate the rate of reaction (rate = 1 ÷ time). A water bath is used to keep the temperature constant so that pH is the only variable being tested. Products of Digestion Once food has been fully digested, the small, soluble molecules are abso

lessons.title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease
lessons.content: The Double Circulatory System The human body uses a double circulatory system . This means blood passes through the heart twice during each full circuit. One loop carries blood from the heart to the lungs and back (the pulmonary circuit), where oxygen is picked up and carbon dioxide is removed. The second loop carries oxygenated blood from the heart to the rest of the body and returns deoxygenated blood back to the heart (the systemic circuit). A double circulatory system is more efficient than a single one because blood returning from the lungs is pumped a second time by the heart before reaching body tissues. This maintains high pressure, ensuring organs receive oxygen quickly enough for aerobic respiration. Key Fact In a double circulatory system, blood enters the heart twice on each journey around the body: once from the lungs (oxygenated) and once from the body (deoxygenated). Structure of the Heart The heart is a muscular organ divided into four chambers. The two upper chambers are called the atria (singular: atrium) and the two lower chambers are the ventricles . The right side of the heart handles deoxygenated blood, while the left side handles oxygenated blood. Valves between the chambers prevent blood from flowing backwards. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle because it needs to pump blood at high pressure all the way around the body. The right ventricle only pumps blood the shorter distance to the lungs. Key Blood Vessels of the Heart Aorta: The largest artery in the body. It carries oxygenated blood away from the left ventricle to the rest of the body. Vena cava: The largest vein. It carries deoxygenated blood from the body back into the right atrium of the heart. Pulmonary artery: Carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. This is unusual because most arteries carry oxygenated blood. Pulmonary vein: Carries oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the left atrium. Again, this is unusual because most veins carry deoxygenated blood. Coronary arteries: Small arteries that branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood and nutrients. Key Fact The natural resting heart rate is controlled by a group of cells in the right atrium that act as a pacemaker . If the natural pacemaker is faulty, an artificial pacemaker — a small electrical device — can be implanted to correct irregular heart rhythms. Types of Blood Vessel The body contains three types of blood vessel, each adapted to its function. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick, elastic, muscular walls to withstand the surge of blood pumped with each heartbeat. Arteries branch into smaller vessels called arterioles, which eventually lead to capillaries. Veins carry blood back towards the heart at low pressure. They have thinner walls than arteries and contain valves to prevent the backflow of blood. Skeletal muscles around veins help squeeze blood along. Capillaries are microscopic vessels only one cell thick. They form networks that pass close to every cell in the body. Their thin walls allow the exchange of substances such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, glucose, and urea between the blood and surrounding tissues by diffusion. Comparing the Three Blood Vessels Arteries: Thick muscular and elastic walls, small lumen, carry blood at high pressure away from the heart. No valves (except where they leave the heart). Veins: Thinner walls with less muscle, larger lumen, carry blood at low pressure towards the heart. Contain valves to prevent backflow. Capillaries: Walls just one cell thick, tiny lumen (red blood cells pass through in single file), allow substance exchange between blood and tissues. Blood and Its Components Blood is classified as a tissue. It consists of four main components, each with a specific role. Plasma is the liquid, straw-coloured part of blood. It makes up about 55% of blood volume. Plasma transports dissolved substances around the body, including glucose and amino acids (to cells), carbon dioxide (to the lungs), urea (to the kidneys for excretion), hormones, and antibodies. Red blood cells transport oxygen from the lungs to body tissues. They are biconcave in shape (like a flattened disc), which increases the surface area to volume ratio for efficient oxygen absorption. Red blood cells contain haemoglobin — a protein that binds with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin, and releases it where oxygen concentration is lower in body tissues. Red blood cells have no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin. White blood cells are part of the immune system. They defend the body against infection by engulfing pathogens (phagocytosis) or producing antibodies and antitoxins. Unlike red blood cells, white blood cells have a nucleus. Platelets are small cell fragments (without a nucleus) that help blood to clot at the site of a wound. Platelets gather at the wound, triggering a cascade of reactions that form a mesh of fibrin threads, creating a scab. This prevents excessive blood loss and stops pathogens from entering. Key Fact Red blood cells are adapted for oxygen transport in three ways: biconcave shape (large surface area), packed with haemoglobin (binds oxygen), and no nucleus (more space for haemoglobin). Coronary Heart Disease Coronary heart disease (CHD) is a non-communicable disease. It occurs when layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries , narrowing them and reducing blood flow. This means the heart muscle receives less oxygen and glucose, which can lead to chest pain (angina) or, in severe cases, a heart attack. Treatments for Coronary Heart Disease Stents: A stent is a small mesh tube inserted into a narrowed coronary artery during surgery. It holds the artery open, restoring normal blood flow. Stents are effective and relatively low risk, but the artery can narrow again over time, and the patient needs to take blood-thinning medication. Statins: These are drugs that reduce blood cholesterol levels, slowing down the rate at which fatty deposits build up inside arteries. Statins must be taken long-term and can cause side effects such as headaches, muscle pain, and liver damage in some patients. Faulty heart valves: If heart valves become faulty — either not opening fully or developing a leak — they can be replaced with biological valves (from human donors or other animals) or mechanical valves (made from metal or polymers). lessons.title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues
lessons.content: Health and Disease Health is defined as a state of physical and mental well-being. It is not simply the absence of disease. Many factors affect health, including diet, stress, and life situations, and these can have a profound effect on both physical and mental well-being. Diseases fall into two broad categories. Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread between organisms. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) cannot be passed from person to person and are often linked to lifestyle or genetic factors. Both types are major causes of ill health worldwide. Key Fact Different types of disease can interact. For example, viruses living in cells can trigger cancers, immune system defects increase susceptibility to infections, immune reactions caused by pathogens can trigger allergies such as asthma, and severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness. Risk Factors for Non-Communicable Diseases Risk factors are linked to an increased rate of a disease. They can be aspects of a person’s lifestyle, substances in their body, or substances in their environment. For some risk factors, a causal mechanism has been scientifically proven. For others, only a correlation has been identified. The specification requires you to know several key risk factor links: Diet, smoking, and exercise affect the risk of cardiovascular disease . A diet high in saturated fat raises blood cholesterol, which can lead to fatty deposits in arteries. Obesity is a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes . Excess body fat can make cells resistant to insulin. Alcohol affects the liver (causing cirrhosis) and brain function (impairing judgement and reaction times). Smoking is a risk factor for lung disease and lung cancer . Tar in cigarettes contains carcinogens that damage lung tissue. Smoking and alcohol during pregnancy affect unborn babies , causing low birth weight, premature birth, and foetal alcohol syndrome. Carcinogens , including ionising radiation (such as UV light and X-rays), are risk factors for cancer . Many non-communicable diseases are caused by the interaction of several factors rather than a single cause. Students must be able to discuss the human and financial cost of NCDs to individuals, local communities, nations, and globally. Human and Financial Costs of Non-Communicable Diseases Human cost: Reduced quality of life, pain, disability, shortened life expectancy, emotional impact on patients and families, mental health consequences such as depression and anxiety. Financial cost: Increased NHS spending on treatment and long-term care, lost working days and reduced productivity, cost of medications and ongoing support, burden on social care services. Globally, NCDs account for the majority of healthcare expenditure in developed countries. Cancer Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division. Normally, cell division is tightly controlled by genes. When these control mechanisms fail — due to mutations in DNA — cells can divide rapidly and form a mass called a tumour . There are two types of tumour. Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells that are contained in one area, usually within a membrane. They do not invade other parts of the body and are not cancerous, though they can cause problems if they press on nearby organs. Malignant tumours are cancers. Their cells invade neighbouring tissues and can spread to different parts of the body in the blood, where they form secondary tumours . This spread of cancer cells is what makes malignant tumours dangerous and potentially fatal. Key Fact Benign tumours = contained, do not spread, not cancer. Malignant tumours = invade other tissues, spread through blood, form secondary tumours, ARE cancer. The key distinction the exam tests is whether the tumour can spread (metastasise). Scientists have identified both lifestyle risk factors (such as smoking, obesity, UV exposure, and drinking alcohol) and genetic risk factors for various types of cancer. Having a risk factor does not guarantee someone will develop cancer — it increases the probability. Comparing Benign and Malignant Tumours Benign: Cells grow slowly, are contained within a membrane, do not spread to other tissues, are not usually life-threatening (unless they press on vital structures such as the brain). Malignant: Cells grow rapidly, invade surrounding healthy tissue, can break away and travel in the blood, form secondary tumours at distant sites, can be life-threatening. Treatment may include surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy. Plant Tissues Just like animals, plants are organised into tissues, organs, and organ systems. A plant tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific function. The specification requires knowledge of five key plant tissues: Epidermal tissue: Covers the outer surface of the plant. It produces a waxy cuticle on leaves to reduce water loss. Palisade mesophyll: Found near the upper surface of the leaf. Packed with chloroplasts for photosynthesis. Spongy mesophyll: Found below the palisade layer. Has air spaces to allow gases (carbon dioxide and oxygen) to diffuse through the leaf. Xylem : Transports water and dissolved mineral ions from roots to stems and leaves. Composed of hollow, dead cells strengthened by lignin. Phloem : Transports dissolved sugars from leaves to the rest of the plant. Composed of elongated living cells with pores in their end walls allowing cell sap to pass through. Meristem tissue is found at the growing tips of shoots and roots. It contains rapidly dividing undifferentiated cells that can develop into any type of plant cell, enabling growth throughout the plant’s life. Key Fact The leaf is a plant organ. For the exam, you must know the tissues within it: epidermis (with waxy cuticle), palisade mesophyll (photosynthesis), spongy mesophyll (gas exchange), xylem and phloem (transport), and guard cells surrounding stomata (control gas exchange and water loss). The Plant Organ System The roots, stem, and leaves form a plant organ system for the transport of substances. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the surface of a plant, mainly through open stomata in the leaves. As water evaporates from the leaf surface, more water is pulled up through the xylem from the roots — this continuous flow is called the transpiration stream . The rate of transpiration is affected by four environmental factors: increasing temperature , decreasing humidity , inc

lessons.title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences
lessons.content: What Are Communicable Diseases? A communicable disease is an illness caused by a pathogen — a microorganism that enters the body and causes infection. Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. They can spread between organisms by direct contact, by water, by air (droplet inhalation) or by vectors such as insects. Once inside the body, bacteria and viruses reproduce rapidly. Bacteria release toxins that damage tissues and make us feel ill. Viruses work differently — they invade living cells, take over the cell’s machinery to make copies of themselves, and destroy the host cell in the process. Key Fact Pathogens are microorganisms that cause infectious disease. The four types are bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. Bacteria produce toxins; viruses damage cells by reproducing inside them. Viral Diseases Measles is caused by a virus spread by inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs. Symptoms include fever and a red skin rash. Measles is a serious illness that can be fatal if complications arise, which is why most young children in the UK are vaccinated against it. HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) initially causes a flu-like illness. It is spread by sexual contact or exchange of body fluids, such as sharing needles. Unless controlled with antiretroviral drugs , HIV attacks the body’s immune cells. Late-stage HIV infection is called AIDS — when the immune system is so damaged it can no longer fight other infections or cancers. Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) is a widespread plant pathogen. It causes a distinctive “mosaic” pattern of discolouration on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and stunting the plant’s growth. Bacterial Diseases: Salmonella & Gonorrhoea Salmonella is a type of food poisoning caused by bacteria. It is spread by eating contaminated food or food prepared in unhygienic conditions. Symptoms include fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea — caused both by the bacteria themselves and the toxins they secrete. In the UK, poultry are vaccinated against Salmonella to help control its spread. Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted disease (STD) caused by a bacterium. Symptoms include a thick yellow or green discharge from the vagina or penis and pain when urinating. It was once easily treated with penicillin, but many antibiotic-resistant strains have now appeared. The spread of gonorrhoea can be reduced by using barrier methods of contraception such as condoms, and by treating infected individuals with antibiotics. Fungal & Protist Diseases Rose black spot is a fungal disease of plants. Purple or black spots develop on leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early. This reduces photosynthesis and slows the plant’s growth. The fungus spreads through the environment by water or wind. It can be treated with fungicides or by removing and destroying affected leaves. Malaria is caused by a protist pathogen. The malarial protist is spread by mosquitoes, which act as vectors — they carry the protist from person to person when they bite. Malaria causes recurrent episodes of fever and can be fatal. Its spread is controlled by preventing mosquitoes from breeding (draining stagnant water) and by using mosquito nets to avoid bites. Human Defence Systems The human body has two lines of defence against pathogens. The first is a set of non-specific defences — physical and chemical barriers that try to stop pathogens entering the body in the first place. Key Fact Non-specific defences include: the skin (acts as a physical barrier), the nose (hairs and mucus trap particles), the trachea and bronchi (lined with mucus and cilia that sweep trapped pathogens to the back of the throat), and the stomach (produces hydrochloric acid that kills most pathogens). The Immune Response If pathogens get past the non-specific defences, the body’s immune system is triggered. White blood cells are the key players in this response. They defend the body in three main ways: 1. phagocytosis — Some white blood cells (phagocytes) detect pathogens and engulf them. They surround the pathogen, take it into the cell and digest it with enzymes. This is a non-specific response — phagocytes attack any invading pathogen. 2. Antibody production — Other white blood cells (lymphocytes) recognise specific antigens on the surface of a pathogen. Each pathogen has unique antigens. The lymphocytes produce specific antibodies that lock onto these antigens and mark the pathogen for destruction. Antibodies are specific — each type only works against one particular pathogen. 3. Antitoxin production — Some white blood cells produce antitoxins that neutralise the toxins produced by bacteria, reducing the damage to tissues. Key Fact White blood cells defend the body by: (1) phagocytosis — engulfing and digesting pathogens, (2) producing antibodies that target specific antigens, and (3) producing antitoxins that neutralise bacterial toxins. How to Reduce the Spread of Disease Different diseases require different prevention strategies. Good hygiene (handwashing, proper food preparation) reduces bacterial spread. Vaccination programmes protect against viral diseases like measles. Using barrier contraception prevents the spread of STDs like gonorrhoea and HIV. Destroying vectors — such as draining standing water where mosquitoes breed — helps control protist diseases like malaria. Isolating infected individuals and quarantine measures also reduce transmission of airborne diseases.

lessons.title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development
lessons.content: Overview This lesson covers three closely linked topics: how vaccination protects individuals and populations, how antibiotics and painkillers are used to treat disease, and how new drugs are discovered, developed and tested before they reach patients. These topics connect directly to the immune response you studied in the previous lesson. Vaccination uses the body’s own defence system, while antibiotics and other drugs work alongside it. Understanding the difference between preventing disease (vaccination), curing disease (antibiotics) and treating symptoms (painkillers) is essential for the exam. How Vaccination Works Vaccination involves introducing a small quantity of dead or inactive forms of a pathogen into the body. These cannot cause the disease, but they carry the same antigens as the live pathogen. When the immune system detects these antigens, white blood cells respond by producing specific antibodies that match the pathogen’s antigens. The crucial advantage of vaccination is immunological memory . After the initial immune response, the body retains memory lymphocytes that “remember” the pathogen’s antigens. If the same pathogen enters the body in the future, these memory cells trigger a much faster and stronger antibody response — destroying the pathogen before it can cause illness. Key Fact Vaccination introduces dead or inactive pathogens → white blood cells produce antibodies → memory lymphocytes remain in the body → if the same pathogen re-enters, antibodies are produced rapidly , preventing infection. The vaccine itself does not cure disease — it trains the immune system to respond. Herd Immunity — Protecting the Whole Population When a large proportion of a population is vaccinated, the spread of the pathogen is significantly reduced because there are fewer people who can become infected and pass it on. This is called herd immunity . It protects people who cannot be vaccinated — such as very young babies, pregnant women, or people with weakened immune systems — because the pathogen cannot find enough hosts to spread through the population. Vaccination programmes have been enormously successful: smallpox was completely eradicated by 1980 through a global vaccination campaign, and diseases like measles, polio and diphtheria have been dramatically reduced. However, if vaccination rates drop, herd immunity is lost and outbreaks can return. Antibiotics and Painkillers Antibiotics , such as penicillin , are medicines that kill infective bacteria inside the body. They have dramatically reduced deaths from bacterial diseases since their widespread use began in the 1940s. It is important to understand that specific bacteria must be treated by specific antibiotics — not all antibiotics work against all types of bacteria. Key Fact Antibiotics kill bacteria but cannot kill viruses. This is because viruses reproduce inside human cells. Destroying the virus would mean destroying the body’s own cells, which is why it is so difficult to develop drugs that target viruses without causing damage to body tissues. Painkillers treat the symptoms of disease (such as pain and fever) but do not kill pathogens. Antibiotic Resistance — A Growing Threat Mutations in bacterial DNA can produce new strains that are antibiotic resistant . When antibiotics are used, non-resistant bacteria are killed but resistant ones survive. These resistant bacteria then reproduce, passing on the resistance gene. Over time, the population of resistant bacteria grows — a process driven by natural selection. MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus ) is a well-known example of an antibiotic-resistant strain. To reduce the development of resistant strains, three measures are essential: Doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately — for example, not for viral infections or non-serious illnesses Patients must complete their full course of antibiotics so all bacteria are killed and none survive to develop resistance Agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted to prevent resistance developing in animal bacteria and transferring to humans The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow, and is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains. This is why preventing resistance is so critical. Discovery and Development of Drugs Traditionally, drugs were extracted from plants and microorganisms. Three important historical examples are: Digitalis — a heart drug originating from foxgloves Aspirin — a painkiller originating from willow bark Penicillin — discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 from the Penicillium mould Today, most new drugs are synthesised by chemists in the pharmaceutical industry. However, the starting point may still be a chemical extracted from a plant or microorganism. The Drug Testing Process — Preclinical and Clinical Trials Before any new drug can be used on patients, it must be extensively tested for three things: toxicity (is it safe?), efficacy (does it work?) and dose (what is the right amount?). The testing process has two stages: Preclinical testing is carried out in a laboratory. The drug is first tested on cells and tissues to check for toxicity, and then on live animals to see how it behaves in a whole organism. This stage identifies drugs that are too dangerous to test on humans. Clinical trials use human volunteers. Very low doses are given at the start to check for safety. If the drug is found to be safe, further trials are carried out at higher doses to find the optimum dose — the amount that is most effective with the fewest side effects. In double blind trials , some patients are given a placebo — a substance that looks identical to the drug but contains no active ingredient. Neither the patient nor the doctor knows who has received the real drug and who has received the placebo. This eliminates bias and ensures that any improvement is genuinely caused by the drug, not by the patient’s belief that they are being treated. Results from clinical trials are only published after they have been checked through peer review — scrutiny by other scientists — to ensure the methods were sound and the conclusions are valid. Key Fact — Drug Testing Stages Preclinical testing (cells, tissues, animals) → Clinical trials (healthy volunteers, then patients) → Low dose first, then optimum dose → Double blind trials with placebos to eliminate bias → Peer review before publication. New drugs are tested for toxicity , efficacy and dose .

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Respiration
lessons.content: Photosynthesis — The Key Reaction Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants and algae make their own food. It takes place in the chloroplasts , which contain the green pigment chlorophyll . Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which is then used to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. The word equation is: Key Fact carbon dioxide + water ⟶ glucose + oxygen In symbols: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O ⟶ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction — energy is transferred from the environment to the chloroplasts by light. You must be able to recognise the chemical symbols CO₂, H₂O, O₂ and C₆H₁₂O₆. The exam may ask you to write the equation in words or symbols, or to identify photosynthesis as endothermic. Rate of Photosynthesis Several factors affect how fast photosynthesis occurs. The three main factors are light intensity , carbon dioxide concentration , and temperature. The amount of chlorophyll also affects the rate — plants with fewer chloroplasts or yellow leaves photosynthesise more slowly. Each of these factors can become a limiting factor . A limiting factor is whichever factor is in shortest supply at a given time. For example, on a bright sunny day, CO₂ concentration may be the limiting factor because there is plenty of light but not enough carbon dioxide for the plant to photosynthesise any faster. How Each Factor Affects the Rate Light intensity: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases — up to a point. Beyond that point, the graph levels off because another factor (such as CO₂ or temperature) becomes limiting. At very low light, photosynthesis stops entirely. Carbon dioxide concentration: Increasing CO₂ concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis until something else becomes limiting. In greenhouses, farmers may add extra CO₂ to boost plant growth. Temperature: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes. As temperature rises, the rate increases because molecules have more kinetic energy. However, above about 40–45°C, enzymes denature and the rate drops sharply to zero. Chlorophyll: Plants affected by disease, mineral deficiency, or genetic conditions may have less chlorophyll, reducing the rate of photosynthesis. Key Fact Required Practical 6: You must know how to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using pondweed. Count oxygen bubbles or measure the volume of gas collected at different distances from a lamp. The independent variable is light intensity (distance from lamp) and the dependent variable is the rate of gas production. Uses of Glucose The glucose produced by photosynthesis is not just used for energy. Plants use it for several purposes: Respiration: Glucose is broken down in respiration to transfer energy for life processes. Storage as starch: Glucose is converted into insoluble starch, which can be stored in leaves, roots, and tubers without affecting water balance. Storage as fats and oils: Seeds often store energy as lipids. Cellulose: Glucose molecules are joined together to make cellulose, which strengthens cell walls. Amino acids and proteins: Glucose is combined with nitrate ions absorbed from the soil to make amino acids, which are then built into proteins. Aerobic Respiration Aerobic respiration is the process of breaking down glucose using oxygen. It happens continuously in every living cell — in both animals and plants. It is an exothermic reaction, meaning it transfers energy to the surroundings. The equation for aerobic respiration is: Key Fact glucose + oxygen ⟶ carbon dioxide + water In symbols: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ ⟶ 6CO₂ + 6H₂O This is the reverse of the photosynthesis equation. Aerobic respiration transfers much more energy than anaerobic respiration. The energy released by respiration is used for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, for movement, and for keeping warm. Respiration is not the same as breathing — breathing is the mechanical process that ventilates the lungs, while respiration is the chemical reaction inside cells. Anaerobic Respiration Anaerobic respiration occurs when cells cannot get enough oxygen. Because the oxidation of glucose is incomplete, far less energy is transferred compared to aerobic respiration. Anaerobic Respiration in Animals vs Plants and Yeast In animal muscles: glucose ⟶ lactic acid. The build-up of lactic acid causes muscles to become fatigued and stop contracting efficiently. An oxygen debt builds up — this is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to break down the accumulated lactic acid in the liver, where it is converted back to glucose. In plants and yeast: glucose ⟶ ethanol + carbon dioxide. This process is called fermentation and has important economic uses: brewing alcoholic drinks and making bread rise (CO₂ creates bubbles in dough). Response to Exercise During exercise, the body’s demand for energy increases. To supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood, the body responds by increasing heart rate, breathing rate, and breath volume (the volume of air in each breath). If the muscles cannot get oxygen fast enough during vigorous exercise, anaerobic respiration takes over. Lactic acid accumulates in the muscles, causing fatigue and pain. After exercise, you continue to breathe heavily to repay the oxygen debt. The blood carries lactic acid to the liver, where oxygen is used to convert it back into glucose. Exam Focus: Oxygen Debt Explained Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells. This is why you pant after sprinting — your body is taking in extra oxygen to break down the lactic acid in the liver. The heart rate and breathing rate remain elevated until the oxygen debt is repaid. Metabolism Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions in a cell or the body. The energy transferred by respiration drives these enzyme-controlled reactions. You need to know the key metabolic processes: Building up (anabolic): Conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen, and cellulose. Formation of lipid molecules from one glycerol and three fatty acids. Use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids, then proteins. Breaking down (catabolic): Respiration itself (breaking glucose down for energy). Breakdown of excess proteins to form urea for excretion by the kidneys (deamination). Key Fact Metabolism links together many topics across the biology specification. Remember: respiration provides the energy for all metabolic r

lessons.title: Culturing Microorganisms and Plant Disease
lessons.content: Culturing Microorganisms Bacteria are grown in laboratories for research, to test the effectiveness of antibiotics and disinfectants, and to study how diseases spread. To grow bacteria, scientists provide the nutrients and conditions they need to reproduce by binary fission — a process where one bacterium splits into two identical cells. Bacteria can be grown in a nutrient broth (a liquid containing dissolved nutrients) or on agar gel plates. Agar is a jelly-like substance extracted from seaweed. When mixed with nutrients and poured into a Petri dish , it sets into a firm surface that bacteria can grow across, forming visible colonies. Key Fact Under ideal conditions, bacteria can divide by binary fission approximately every 20 minutes. Starting from one bacterium, this means there could be over 1 million bacteria after just 7 hours. Aseptic Technique When culturing bacteria, it is essential to prevent contamination by unwanted microorganisms. Aseptic technique is the set of precautions taken to ensure that only the desired bacteria grow on the agar plate. Contamination could introduce harmful pathogens or produce unreliable results. Steps in Aseptic Technique 1. Sterilise equipment: The Petri dish, agar, and all equipment must be sterilised before use. The inoculating loop is sterilised by passing it through a hot Bunsen burner flame until it glows red. This kills any bacteria already on the loop. 2. Allow the loop to cool: After sterilising, the inoculating loop must be allowed to cool in the air without touching any surfaces. Placing it on the bench would pick up contaminants. 3. Transfer the bacteria: The lid of the bacterial culture bottle is briefly removed and the neck of the bottle is passed through the Bunsen flame to kill any microorganisms around the opening. The cooled loop is dipped into the culture to pick up bacteria. 4. Inoculate the agar plate: The lid of the Petri dish is lifted slightly — not removed completely — and the bacteria are spread in a zigzag pattern across the agar surface. The lid is replaced quickly to minimise exposure to airborne microorganisms. 5. Seal and incubate: The Petri dish is secured with two pieces of tape (not sealed all the way round, to allow air in and prevent the growth of anaerobic pathogens). The plate is stored upside down to stop condensation dripping onto the colonies. Key Fact In school laboratories, agar plates are incubated at a maximum of 25°C. This is because higher temperatures (such as 37°C, used in industry) could encourage the growth of harmful human pathogens. At 25°C, bacteria still grow but dangerous species are less likely to thrive. Investigating Antibiotics — Zones of Inhibition One key application of culturing bacteria is the required practical that investigates the effect of antibiotics or disinfectants on bacterial growth. Different substances are compared by measuring how effectively they prevent bacteria from growing. In this experiment, filter paper discs are soaked in different antibiotics or disinfectants and placed on an agar plate that has been inoculated with bacteria (a “bacterial lawn”). A control disc soaked in distilled water is also placed on the plate. After incubation, clear areas appear around the discs where the substance has killed or prevented bacterial growth. These clear areas are called zones of inhibition . The larger the zone of inhibition, the more effective the antibiotic or disinfectant is against that particular type of bacterium. However, a large zone does not mean the substance is effective against all bacteria — it may be useless against a different species. To calculate the area of a zone of inhibition, measure the diameter of the clear zone in mm, halve it to get the radius, and use the formula: \(area = πr^{2}\) . If the zone is not perfectly circular, measure the diameter in two directions and use the mean. Worked Example: Calculating a Zone of Inhibition A zone of inhibition has a diameter of 20 mm. The radius is 20 ÷ 2 = 10 mm. The area = π × 10² = 3.14 × 100 = \(314 mm^{2}\) . If the diameters measured in two directions were 20 mm and 18 mm, the mean diameter = (20 + 18) ÷ 2 = 19 mm. Radius = 9.5 mm. Area = π × 9.5² = 3.14 × 90.25 = \(283 mm^{2}\) . Plant Disease Plants can be infected by a range of pathogens including viruses, bacteria, fungi, and insects. Plant disease can reduce crop yields and threaten food security, so detecting and identifying diseases early is critical. Examples of Plant Diseases Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV): A virus that causes a distinctive mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves. This reduces the amount of chlorophyll available for photosynthesis, stunting the plant’s growth. Rose black spot: A fungal disease that causes purple or black spots on leaves. Infected leaves turn yellow and drop early, reducing photosynthesis. It spreads through water and wind. Aphids: Aphids are small insects that feed on plant sap from the phloem. They weaken the plant by removing sugars and amino acids, and can act as vectors, transmitting viral diseases from one plant to another. Detecting Plant Disease Plant diseases can be detected in several ways. Gardeners, farmers, and scientists look for visible signs such as stunted growth, spots or lesions on leaves, areas of decay or rot, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration, and the presence of pests. These symptoms help narrow down the possible cause. To confirm a diagnosis, scientists can use identification keys (dichotomous keys that guide users through a series of yes/no questions), testing kits that detect specific pathogens using monoclonal antibodies, or laboratory analysis including DNA testing or culturing the pathogen. Ion Deficiency in Plants Sometimes what looks like disease is actually caused by a mineral ion deficiency . Plants absorb mineral ions from the soil through their roots by active transport, and a shortage of key minerals produces distinctive symptoms. Nitrate deficiency: Nitrate ions are needed to make amino acids and proteins. Without enough nitrate, the plant cannot grow properly and shows stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves (chlorosis). Magnesium deficiency: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll. Without enough magnesium, leaves turn yellow because chlorophyll cannot be produced, reducing photosynthesis. Key Fact Nitrate is needed for protein synthesis (making amino acids), so deficiency causes stunted growth. Magnesium is needed for chlorophyll production, so defi

lessons.title: Monoclonal Antibodies
lessons.content: What Are Monoclonal Antibodies? Your immune system produces antibodies to fight pathogens. Each antibody is specific — it only binds to one type of antigen . Normally, your body produces many different antibodies at once (polyclonal antibodies). But scientists have found a way to produce large quantities of a single, identical antibody. These are called monoclonal antibodies . Monoclonal antibodies are incredibly useful because they are all identical and all target the same specific protein or cell. This makes them precise tools for diagnosis, research and treatment. Key Fact Monoclonal antibodies are produced from a single clone of cells. “Mono” means one and “clonal” means from a clone — so monoclonal antibodies are all identical copies that bind to one specific antigen. How Are Monoclonal Antibodies Produced? Producing monoclonal antibodies involves combining two types of cell to create a hybridoma . Here is the step-by-step process: Step 1 Inject the antigen A mouse is injected with the specific antigen that you want to produce antibodies against. The mouse’s immune system responds by producing lymphocytes that make antibodies against that antigen. Step 2 Extract lymphocytes The antibody-producing lymphocytes are extracted from the mouse. These cells can make the right antibody, but they cannot divide indefinitely on their own. Step 3 Fuse with tumour cells The lymphocytes are fused with tumour cells (cancer cells). Detergent is added to break down the cell-surface membranes so the cells can fuse together. Tumour cells are used because they divide rapidly and do not stop dividing. Step 4 Create hybridoma cells The fused cells are called hybridoma cells. They combine the lymphocyte’s ability to produce a specific antibody with the tumour cell’s ability to divide indefinitely. Step 5 Select and clone The hybridoma cells are separated and tested. Only those producing the desired antibody are selected. These are then grown on a large scale in culture, and the monoclonal antibodies are collected from the growth medium. Why Use Tumour Cells? Lymphocytes can produce antibodies but cannot divide for very long. Once a lymphocyte becomes a B lymphocyte and starts producing antibodies, it loses the ability to divide. Tumour cells, on the other hand, divide uncontrollably — that is what makes cancer dangerous. By fusing the two, scientists get a cell that does both: produces antibodies and divides indefinitely. Uses of Monoclonal Antibodies Monoclonal antibodies have several important applications in medicine and research. Because they bind to one specific antigen, they can be used to target particular molecules or cells with great precision. Pregnancy Testing One of the most familiar uses of monoclonal antibodies is the pregnancy test . When a woman becomes pregnant, her body produces the hormone HCG (human chorionic gonadotrophin). This hormone is excreted in urine. The pregnancy test strip contains monoclonal antibodies that are designed to bind specifically to HCG. If HCG is present in the urine sample, it binds to the monoclonal antibodies on the strip. These antibody-HCG complexes move along the strip and bind to a second set of immobilised antibodies at the test line, producing a visible colour change. A positive result shows two lines; a negative result shows only one (the control line). Blood and Laboratory Testing Monoclonal antibodies are used in laboratory blood tests to measure levels of specific hormones, detect pathogens, or identify blood groups. Because they bind only to one target, they provide very accurate and reliable results. For example, they can detect the presence of a specific virus in a patient’s blood sample. Key Fact Monoclonal antibodies are used in pregnancy tests to detect the hormone HCG, in laboratory blood tests to identify pathogens or measure hormone levels, and in research to locate specific molecules in cells. Research In scientific research, monoclonal antibodies are used to identify and locate specific molecules within cells or tissues. Because each monoclonal antibody targets one specific protein, researchers can use them like molecular labels — attaching a fluorescent marker to the antibody and then tracking where the target molecule appears in the body or in a tissue sample. Monoclonal Antibodies in Cancer Treatment Cancer cells have specific antigens on their surface that normal cells do not. Scientists can design monoclonal antibodies to bind to these cancer-specific antigens. Once bound, the antibodies can: Trigger the patient’s own immune system to attack the cancer cells Carry a radioactive substance, toxic drug or chemical directly to the cancer cell, killing it without harming surrounding healthy tissue (this is sometimes called a “magic bullet”) Block chemical signals that tell the cancer cell to divide This targeted approach causes fewer side effects than traditional chemotherapy, which kills all rapidly dividing cells — including healthy ones like hair follicle cells and cells lining the gut. Problems and Ethical Issues Although monoclonal antibodies were initially expected to be a “magic bullet” for treating many diseases, they have created more side effects than expected. Some of the issues include: Side effects: Monoclonal antibodies can cause unexpected immune reactions in patients. In 2006, a clinical trial of the monoclonal antibody TGN1412 caused six healthy volunteers to suffer multiple organ failure within minutes, likely because T cells overproduced chemicals that stimulated a massive immune response. Animal use: Production involves using mice — both to produce antibodies and to create tumour cells. Inducing cancer in mice raises ethical concerns, even with guidelines in place to minimise suffering. Genetic engineering: Transgenic mice can be used (with a human gene inserted) so that they produce human antibodies rather than mouse antibodies. This avoids the need to “humanise” the antibodies, but raises separate ethical issues about genetic engineering. The TGN1412 Trial — A Case Study In March 2006, six healthy volunteers in London took part in a clinical trial of a new monoclonal antibody called TGN1412. Within minutes of receiving the drug, all six suffered multiple organ failure. The volunteers survived, but the incident raised serious questions about the safety of drug trials and whether trials should only involve patients who are already ill with the condition the drug is designed to treat.
